title: Published breeding-season climate effects did not forecast eastern monarch winter colony area in 2015-2025, and the two selected climate terms reversed sign after 2014
abstract: Question: Do published climate effects on the eastern monarch butterfly forecast the winter colony area in Mexico after the end of the original fits? Method: We fitted models on the winters 1994-95 to 2014-15, froze them, and forecast the 11 winters 2015-16 to 2025-26 (WWF-Mexico/CONANP area). Covariates came from NOAA nClimGrid-daily state means, MODIS NDVI and USGS glyphosate estimates. We also used rolling-origin forecasts for 2005-2025, period-interaction tests of each slope, and a permutation test of climate-term selection. Results: The two climate terms of Thogmartin et al. (2017), cold August nights and warm days on 1-10 May in the north-central US, increased the forecast mean squared error by 31-61% with the published slopes and by 23-89% when refitted against matched no-climate baselines. Both slopes changed sign after 2014 (change p = 0.007 and 0.025). A BIC search over 38 climate candidates found the early-May term again, but its in-sample R2 gain (0.185) did not exceed the gain from permuted climate years (p = 0.12). Terms with a direct mechanism (autumn Texas-Oklahoma NDVI, June temperature and degree days in the north-central US) kept a stable positive sign but gave small gains that did not repeat in rolling-origin forecasts (MSE skill -0.19 to +0.21). Spring rain in Texas had the opposite sign to the published effect. The population did not continue to decrease after 2014 (geometric mean 1.60 ha in 2010-2014, 2.56 ha in 2015-2025); a cumulative-glyphosate term forecast a continued decrease. No model reliably improved on persistence or a 5-year mean. We give a forecast for winter 2026-27 of about 2 ha (80% interval 0.8-4.7 ha). Limitations: 11 test winters; area is a proxy for abundance; the NABA summer index of Saunders et al. (2019) is not public; covariates are reconstructions of the published definitions.
